cards.explanation: The answer is that Joash listens to them. The officials of Judah come and pay homage, and the verse says, “…and he listened to them.” Friends, I can be talked into anything by one person who says my cookies look nice. So I won't pretend I'd have done better.

The answer is False. Verse 18 says, “They abandoned the house of the LORD, the God of their fathers, and served the Asherah poles and idols.” That's about as far from faithful as it gets. I think this is one of those spots where you just wish somebody had said, “Hold on, let's think about this.”

The word is wrath. The text says they abandoned the house of the LORD and served the Asherah poles and idols. Then it says, “So wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem for this guilt of theirs.” That little “So” ties the wrath to what they had just done, and I think that's worth slowing down for, because the text doesn't leave us guessing why it came.

The word is listen. Verse 19 says the LORD sent prophets “…to bring the people back to Him and to testify against them, but they would not listen.” The prophets came to bring them back, and the people would not listen. I think it stings, friends, when you say something and nobody looks up.

The answer is prospering. Zechariah, son of Jehoiada the priest, stands before the people and says, “Why do you transgress the commandments of the LORD so that you cannot prosper?” (2 Chronicles 24:20). He opens with a question and he says what it costs them. I think it's a very direct way to start a message.

The answer is True. Zechariah says, “Because you have forsaken the LORD, He has forsaken you.” The people left the LORD, and the message says the LORD has left them. It's a short sentence that carries a lot of weight, friends.

The answer is False. The verse says, “But they conspired against Zechariah, and by order of the king, they stoned him in the courtyard of the house of the LORD.” The order came from King Joash. It's a heavy part of the story, friends.

The word is kindness. Verse 22 says, “Thus King Joash failed to remember the kindness that Zechariah’s father Jehoiada had extended to him.” Jehoiada had shown Joash kindness, and Joash killed Jehoiada's son. I think that's one of the saddest lines in the passage.

Zechariah asks the LORD to see it and call Joash to account. As he lay dying, he said, “May the LORD see this and call you to account.” (2 Chronicles 24:22). The text gives those words right after it says Joash killed Jehoiada's son. I think this one hurts, friends.

The answer is True. Verse 23 says the army of Aram “…entered Judah and Jerusalem and destroyed all the leaders of the people…” They also sent all the plunder to their king in Damascus. That's a heavy sentence, friends, and it means what it says.

The answer is that the LORD hands Judah's army to them. Verse 24 says, “Although the Aramean army had come with only a few men, the LORD delivered into their hand a very great army.” Few men, a very great army, and the verse says the LORD is the one who delivered it. It also gives the reason: “Because Judah had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers, judgment was executed on Joash.”

The answer is Joash. Verse 24 says, “Because Judah had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers, judgment was executed on Joash.” The king of Judah is the one the text names. It's a sober line, friends.

The word is servants. Verse 25 says, “His own servants conspired against him…” These are the people who worked for the king, and they turn on him while he's wounded. It's a hard turn in the story, friends.

The reason is for shedding the blood of Jehoiada's son. Verse 25 says, “His own servants conspired against him for shedding the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest…” Zechariah was that son. What Joash did to him comes back around, friends.

The answer is False. Verse 25 says he “…was buried in the City of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.” So he's buried in the City of David, just not in the tombs of the kings. It's a small detail, friends, and it says a lot.
